**Given:** The qubit computational basis and the diagonal states and maps in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-it-finite-dimensional-quantum-relative-entropy]]: $D(A\|B)$ is the natural-log spectral expression under support inclusion and equals $+\infty$ when support inclusion fails.

[F2] [[def-qc-fidelity]]: root fidelity is $F(\rho,\sigma)=\|\sqrt\rho\sqrt\sigma\|_1$.

[F3] [[def-qc-trace-distance]]: trace distance is $d_{\rm tr}(\rho,\sigma)=\frac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1$.

[F4] [[def-qc-trace-norm]]: the trace norm is the sum of the singular values.

[F5] [[def-qc-density-operator]]: a density operator is nonnegative and has trace one.

[F6] [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]: positive diagonal operators have the diagonal positive square roots obtained by taking square roots of their eigenvalues.

[F7] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: the natural logarithm is defined on positive reals, is strictly increasing, and obeys the usual logarithm laws.

[F8] [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]]: sine is strictly increasing on $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$.

[F9] [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]: $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and $\cos(\pi/2)=0$.

[F10] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]]: sine and cosine satisfy their addition formulas, including $\sin(u-v)=\sin u\cos v-\cos u\sin v$ and $\cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v$.

[F11] [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]: $\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$ for every real $t$.

[F12] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]: $(\sin t)'=\cos t$ and $\cos' t=-\sin t$.

[F13] [[thm-chain-rule]] and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: the chain and product rules permit two differentiations of the displayed trigonometric identity.

[F14] [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]: differentiability of cosine implies continuity at the endpoint limit used below.

[F15] [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]]: $\pi$ is positive, so the intervals and angles in the Statement have the stated order.



1.1 For $\theta\in[a,\pi/4]$, $\rho_{\sin^2\theta}=\operatorname{diag}(\cos^2\theta,\sin^2\theta)$ is nonnegative and has trace one by [F11], so is a state by [F5]. Since $a>0$ by [F15], [F8] and [F12] make sine positive and strictly increasing on $[a,\pi/4]$; squaring preserves strict order there, so the angle parametrization is injective and $T_a$ is well-defined. Its output angle lies in $[0,\pi/4-a]$, so its output is also a density operator. [given, F5, F8, F11, F12, F15, algebra]

1.2 If a quantum channel agreed with $T_a$ on $\mathcal S_a$, complex-linearity would make its output's $|1\rangle$ diagonal entry affine in $p$, since $\rho_p=(1-p)|0\rangle\langle0|+p|1\rangle\langle1|$. Thus there would be constants $A,B$ with $\sin^2(\theta-a)=A+B\sin^2\theta$ for every $\theta\in[a,\pi/4]$. Differentiating twice on the open interval and using [F10]–[F13] gives $\cos(2\theta-2a)=B\cos(2\theta)$. By [F14], cosine is continuous, so taking $\theta\uparrow\pi/4$ yields $\sin(2a)=0$, because $\cos(\pi/2-2a)=\sin(2a)$ and $\cos(\pi/2)=0$. But $0<2a=\pi/6<\pi/2$ by [F15], so [F8]–[F9] give $\sin(2a)>0$, a contradiction. Hence no quantum channel agrees with $T_a$ on the family. [given, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, F13, F14, F15, algebra]

2.1 For $\theta,\phi\in[a,\pi/4]$, the square roots in [F6] are diagonal with entries $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ and $(\cos\phi,\sin\phi)$. Their product is positive diagonal, so by [F2] and [F4], $$F(\rho_{\sin^2\theta},\rho_{\sin^2\phi})=\cos\theta\cos\phi+\sin\theta\sin\phi=\cos(\theta-\phi).$$ The cosine addition formula [F10] justifies the last equality. Applying $T_a$ subtracts $a$ from both angles, leaving their difference unchanged; root fidelity is therefore preserved for every pair. [given, F2, F4, F6, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For diagonal qubit states, [F3] and [F4] give $d_{\rm tr}(\rho_p,\rho_q)=|p-q|$. Take $\theta\ge\phi$ in $[a,\pi/4]$. The addition formulas and Pythagorean identity [F10]–[F11] give $\sin^2u-\sin^2v=\sin(u+v)\sin(u-v)$. Therefore $$\sin^2\theta-\sin^2\phi=\sin(\theta+\phi)\sin(\theta-\phi),$$ $$\sin^2(\theta-a)-\sin^2(\phi-a)=\sin(\theta+\phi-2a)\sin(\theta-\phi).$$ Here $0\le\theta+\phi-2a\le\theta+\phi\le\pi/2$, so [F8]–[F12] make the first sine factor in the second line no larger than the corresponding nonnegative factor in the first line; the other factor is the same and nonnegative. Thus the output coordinate difference is at most the input difference, proving trace-distance contraction for every pair. [given, F3, F4, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 Take $\theta=\pi/4$ and $\phi=a$. By strict increase of sine from $\sin0=0$ to $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ in [F8], [F9], and [F12], every angle strictly between zero and $\pi/2$ gives $0<\sin^2\theta<1$; thus both input diagonal states have full support and their relative entropy is finite by [F1] and [F7], since the positive spectral entries have finite natural logarithms. The outputs are $\rho_{\sin^2(\pi/4-a)}$ and $\rho_0=|0\rangle\langle0|$. Since $0<\pi/4-a<\pi/2$ by [F15], the first output has full support, while the second has one-dimensional support; support inclusion fails and [F1] gives output divergence $+\infty$. [given, F1, F7, F8, F9, F12, F15, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Independently, the root fidelity of $|0\rangle\langle0|$ and $|+\rangle\langle+|$ is $1/\sqrt2$: the product of their positive square roots is $(1/\sqrt2)|0\rangle\langle+|$, whose only nonzero singular value is $1/\sqrt2$. Their difference is $\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, whose square is $I/2$, so both singular values are $1/\sqrt2$ and [F3]–[F4] give trace distance $1/\sqrt2$. The first support is not contained in the second, so [F1] gives infinite relative entropy. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The rank-one Coxeter system $W=S_2$, the universal Hecke algebra over its Laurent parameter ring, and the specializations $q=i$, $q=1$, and $q=-1$ over $\mathbb C$.

[F1] [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]: the rank-one quadratic relation is $(T-v)(T+v^{-1})=0$ for a unit parameter $v$.

[F2] [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]]: arbitrary scalar extension presents the specialized Hecke algebra by the images of the same quadratic and braid relations, with no flatness assumption.

[A1] $i^2=-1$, so $i^{-1}=-i$ and $i$ is a unit in $\mathbb C$.

[A2] The values $1$ and $-1$ are units in $\mathbb C$ and each has square $1$.



1.1 For any unit $q$, expanding [F1] and putting $S=qT$ gives $S^2=(q^2-1)S+q^2$, equivalently $(S-q^2)(S+1)=0$; thus the multiplicative source parameter is $\xi=q^2$, while all calculations below keep the local $T$ generator. Now set $q=i$. Then [F1] gives $(T-i)(T+i^{-1})=(T-i)^2=0$, and [F2] identifies this as the complete specialized presentation. With $\epsilon=T-i$, translation $T=\epsilon+i$ gives mutually inverse homomorphisms between $H_2(i)$ and $\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. Every class has a unique form $a+b\epsilon$: terms of degree at least two vanish, and a polynomial of degree at most one lying in $(\epsilon^2)$ has both coefficients zero. Hence the algebra has basis $1,\epsilon$ and $\epsilon$ is nonzero. [given, F1, F2, A1, algebra, construct]

1.2 For $q=1$ and $q=-1$, [F1] gives the same relation $T^2-1=0$, using [F2] for the specialization. The elements $e_+=(1+T)/2$ and $e_-=(1-T)/2$ are orthogonal idempotents with sum $1$. The classes $1,T$ are linearly independent because no nonzero polynomial of degree at most one is divisible by $T^2-1$, so $e_+$ and $e_-$ are nonzero and form a basis. Thus $H_2(q)=\mathbb C e_+\oplus\mathbb C e_-$, and each one-dimensional left ideal is simple. The regular module is semisimple. [given, F1, F2, A2, algebra, construct]

2.1 The left ideal $\epsilon H_2(i)$ is one-dimensional, nonzero and proper by step 1.1, so the left regular module is not simple. If it were a direct sum of simple left ideals, its dimension two would force it to be a sum of two one-dimensional simple modules. On any one-dimensional module, left multiplication by $\epsilon$ is a scalar $\lambda$ satisfying $\lambda^2=0$, hence $\lambda=0$. It would then annihilate both summands and therefore all of $H_2(i)$, contradicting $\epsilon\cdot1=\epsilon\ne0$. Thus the regular module is not semisimple. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Steps 2.1 and 1.2 establish the two different specialization outcomes under the stated normalized relation. They make no claim about higher ranks, centralizers, positive characteristic, or every root of unity. No choice principle is used: every basis, idempotent, and module complement calculation is explicit and finite. [step 2.1, step 1.2, given] ∎
